To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) NF2 point mutations in tumour samples are common in young patients with vestibular schwannomata and that 2) the identification of both truncating mutations in tumour DNA and the absence of these mutations in blood DNA is a useful predictor of the absence of NF2 in family members.

(1) NF2 mutations in blood samples cannot be used to predict which individuals with unilateral vestibular tumours are likely to develop further NF2-related tumours, and; (2) the identification of both mutations (or one mutation and LOH) in the tumour DNA of a patient with a vestibular schwannom and exclusion of these mutations from the blood of their sibs or offspring is sufficient to render further surveillance unnecessary in these individuals.

(1) molecular genetic analysis of the blood of young patients with unilateral tumour is not useful in identifying those at risk of NF2, (2) tumour analysis can be used to identify those at risk of further tumours, and, (3) the presence of both mutations or the presence of one mutation plus LO in the tumour but not the blood may be sufficient to identify those at no risk of developing further disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular genetic analysis of the neurofibromatosis 2 gene in young people presenting with a vestibular schwannom.
understanding the molecular basis of tumour development in patients with NF2.
the molecular genetic basis of NF2, a rare genetic disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular analysis of tumour and blood samples is not yet a reliable means of identifying those individuals at risk of developing tumours.
NF2 is not the cause of the vestibular schwanna in these patients, but the possibility of mosaicism cannot be excluded.

NF2 mutations are not identified in blood DNA of young patients with unilateral tumours, that NF2 mutations and/or LOH are identified in 75% of tumour DNA, that 65% of tumours have both NF2 mutations, and that in one patient with a multilobular schwannoma, the first hit mutation was common to all lobes but the second mutational hit differed in the different tumour lobes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

molecular genetic analysis of the vestibular schwanna is useful in predicting the risk to other family members of developing NF2 but is not useful in predicting the future development of bilateral vestibular schwannas in the index case.
molecular genetic analysis is a useful adjunct in the clinical management of young patients with unilateral tumours, but that the clinical diagnosis of NF2 should not be based on this alone.
in the majority of patients with unilateral vestibulocochlear schwannomas, the NF2 gene is inactivated through somatic mutation.
